summary: In dense topologies, link-state flooding can slow down convergence. This experimental document discusses the problem and an architectural solution that shrinks the flooding topology, and specifies protocol changes for IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

plainLanguage.summary: In a network where every router is connected to every other router, a routing update has to reach everyone, and the usual way of spreading it sends it many redundant copies. This RFC says to pick a smaller set of links that still reaches everybody, and to flood updates only along that set.

questions: dynamic flooding in is-is and ospf
how to reduce link-state flooding in dense networks
how does dynamic flooding improve convergence
subtitle: Restricting link-state flooding to a smaller graph inside a dense network.

tldr.problem: In a dense topology such as a data centre spine-leaf fabric, link-state flooding sends the same update to every node many times, which overloads the control plane and slows convergence.
tldr.mechanism: The routers agree on a much smaller graph, the flooding topology, that still reaches every node, and flood only along that graph; it is computed either centrally by an elected Area Leader or locally by every node using the same algorithm.
tldr.outcome: The flooding topology covers all reachable nodes and can be a simple cycle, and the document gives concrete constructions for complete bipartite topologies along with the protocol encodings for IS-IS and OSPF.

today: RFC 9667 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document says the trade-offs between graph diameter, node degree, convergence time and topology computation time are for further study, and asks for the operational experience that would be needed before the approach advances.

sections.title: The Problem with Dense Topologies
sections.content:
There has been increased focus on the dynamic routing of networks with a bipartite, also known as spine-leaf or leaf-spine, Clos or Fat-tree topology. Conventional Interior Gateway Protocols, that is IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, underperform in these networks, redundantly flooding information throughout the dense topology, which leads to overloaded control plane inputs and creates operational issues. For practical considerations, some network architects have resorted to applying BGP in the data centre. However, some feel that using an Exterior Gateway Protocol as an IGP is suboptimal, perhaps only because of the configuration overhead.

The primary issue is the poor reaction of the network to topology changes. Normal link-state routing protocols rely on a flooding algorithm for state distribution within an area. In a dense topology this flooding algorithm is highly redundant and results in unnecessary overhead. Each node receives each link state update multiple times. All the redundant copies are eventually discarded, but only after they have reached the control plane and been processed. This creates issues because significant Link State Database updates can become queued behind many redundant copies of another update, which delays convergence as the database does not stabilize promptly.

In a real implementation, the packet queues leading to the control plane are necessarily of finite size, so if the flooding rate exceeds the update processing rate for long enough, the control plane must drop incoming updates. If those lost updates matter, this further delays the stabilization of the database and the convergence of the network.

This is not a new problem. Historically, when routing protocols were deployed where the underlying topology was a complete graph, there were similar issues. This was more common when the link-layer fabric presented the network layer with a full mesh of virtual connections. It was addressed by reducing the flooding topology through IS-IS Mesh Groups, but that approach requires careful configuration.

The root problem is therefore not limited to massively scalable data centres; it exists with any dense topology at scale. Link-state routing protocols were conceived when links were very expensive and topologies were sparse. Technology has progressed to the point where links are cheap and common, which reverses the economic fundamentals of network engineering. The original designs are to be commended for continuing to provide correct operation, and optimizations for today's environment are to be expected.
sections.plainLanguage: In a network where every router is connected to every other router, a routing update has to reach everyone, and the usual way of spreading it sends it many redundant copies. This RFC says to pick a smaller set of links that still reaches everybody, and to flood updates only along that set.

sections.title: Solution Requirements
sections.content:
A solution to this problem must meet six requirements.

  • It must provide a dynamic routing solution: reachability must be restored after any topology change.
  • It must provide a significant improvement in convergence.
  • It should address a variety of dense topologies. Addressing only a complete bipartite topology such as K5,8 is insufficient; multi-stage Clos topologies must also be addressed, as well as topologies that are slight variants. Addressing complete graphs is a good demonstration of generality.
  • There must be no single point of failure: the loss of any link or node should not unduly hinder convergence.
  • The workload for flooding should be evenly distributed. A hot spot, where one node has an extreme workload, would be a performance limitation and a vulnerability for resiliency.
  • Dense topologies are subgraphs of much larger topologies, and operational efficiency requires that the dense subgraph not operate in a radically different manner than the remainder of the topology. Any change to any node outside the dense subgraph is not acceptable, since a massively scaled data centre may be part of a larger wide-area network, and a second protocol operating only on the subgraph would add much more complexity at the edge where the two protocols would have to interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has to keep working when links and routers fail, spread the flooding work evenly instead of overloading one router, work on many shapes of dense network, and be able to sit inside a bigger network without changing anything outside it.

sections.title: Dynamic Flooding
sections.content:
The combination of a dense topology and flooding on the physical topology is suboptimal for network scaling. However, if the flooding topology is decoupled from the physical topology and restricted to a greatly reduced portion of it, the result can be efficient flooding and the resilience of existing protocols. A node that supports flooding on the decoupled flooding topology is said to support dynamic flooding.

The flooding topology is computed within an IGP area with the dense topology, either centrally on an elected node, termed the Area Leader, or in a distributed manner on all nodes that support dynamic flooding. In the centralized mode, the flooding topology is encoded into and distributed as part of the normal Link State Database. In the distributed mode, it is computed locally. Nodes within such an area flood only on the flooding topology. On links outside the flooding topology, normal database synchronization mechanisms, that is OSPF database exchange and IS-IS Complete Sequence Number PDUs, apply, but flooding may not.

New link-state information arriving from outside the flooding topology suggests that the sender has no flooding topology information or is operating on old information about it, so it should be flooded on the flooding topology as well. The flooding topology covers the full set of nodes within the area but excludes some of the links that standard flooding would employ. Since it is computed before topology changes, the effort required to compute it does not factor into the convergence time and can be done when the topology is stable.

Graph theory defines the degree of a node as the number of edges attached to it. To keep the flooding workload scalable and distributed, there should be no nodes in the flooding topology with a much higher degree than others. A node that has no flooding topology information when it receives new link-state information should flood according to standard flooding rules, which occurs when the dense topology is first established but is unlikely to recur.

Link-state protocols are intentionally designed to be asynchronous with nodes acting independently. During flooding, different nodes have different information, producing transient conditions that can temporarily cause suboptimal forwarding. When centralized mode is used and multiple flooding topologies are advertised during a transient, nodes should flood link-state updates on all of them, each node first evaluating the election of the Area Leader locally and flooding on its flooding topology first. The rationale is that during a transient with a recent change of Area Leader, propagating topology information promptly along the most likely flooding topology should be the priority.

During transients, loops may form in the flooding topology. This is not problematic, as the standard flooding rules cause duplicate updates to be ignored. The flooding topology may also become disconnected, which is handled by the rules for topology events.

The flooding topology is encoded as a set of intersecting paths, where each path is a set of connected links. A simple list of nodes would suffice for a pure cycle but would need a different scheme as soon as one extra link was added. Advertisement of the flooding topology supports multi-access broadcast LANs: when a LAN is included, all edges between the LAN and the nodes connected to it are assumed to be part of the flooding topology, so explicit advertisement of these edges is optional. That can produce hidden or stealth nodes, which are part of the flooding topology but not explicitly mentioned in the advertisements; they can be found by examining the Link State Database.

Correct operation requires that all participating nodes choose local links for flooding that are part of the calculated flooding topology. To help diagnose problems, the document defines a means of advertising the Local Edges Enabled for Flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: The routers agree on a smaller graph that still reaches everybody, and flood updates only along that graph. It can be worked out by one elected router and published to everyone, or worked out independently by every router using an agreed algorithm. In both cases the result is the same set of links.

sections.title: Flooding Topologies on Complete Bipartite Graphs
sections.content:
There is a great deal of flexibility in how the flooding topology may be computed. For resiliency it needs at least to contain a cycle of all nodes in the dense subgraph, though additional links could be added to decrease the convergence time. The trade-off between density and convergence time is a matter for further study. The exact algorithm for the centralized case need not be standardized, as it is not an interoperability issue; only the encoding of the resultant topology needs to be documented. In the distributed case, all nodes in the area need to use the same algorithm, and private algorithms are allowed so long as all nodes agree.

While the flooding topology should be a covering cycle, it need not be a Hamiltonian cycle where each node appears only once. In many relevant topologies this will not be possible, for example K5,8. This is fortunate, because computing a Hamiltonian cycle is known to be NP-complete. A simple algorithm for a complete bipartite graph is to select unvisited nodes on each side until both sides are completely visited. If the numbers of nodes on each side are unequal, revisiting nodes on the less populated side is inevitable. This algorithm runs in O(N) time.

While a simple cycle is adequate for correctness and resiliency, it may not be optimal for convergence. At scale a cycle may have a diameter that is half the number of nodes in the graph, which could cause an undue delay in link-state update propagation. Introducing more links would reduce the diameter at the trade-off of possibly adding redundant messaging, so it may be useful to have a bound on the diameter. Similarly, if additional redundancy is added, specific nodes may end up with a very high degree, which could overload their control plane. It may therefore be preferable to have an upper bound on the degree of nodes in the flooding topology.

A minimal flooding topology on a complete bipartite graph is one in which the topology is connected and each node has at least degree two, which guarantees no single point of failure. In practice this means every leaf node has a degree of two. As there are usually more leaves than spines, the degree of the spines will be higher, but the load on individual spines can be evenly distributed. This type also scales well: for N spines and M leaves, if M is at least N(N/2-1), there is a flooding topology with a diameter of 4.

A Xia topology on a complete bipartite graph is one in which all spine nodes are biconnected through leaves with degree two, but the remaining leaves all have degree one and are evenly distributed across the spines. Constructively, one iterates through the spines, connecting each spine to the next by selecting any unused leaf. Because leaves are connected to all spines, any leaf can be chosen without loss of generality. Continuing across all spines and selecting a new leaf at each iteration results in a path connecting all spines, and adding one more leaf between the last and first spine produces a cycle of N spines and N leaves. The remaining M minus N leaves are distributed evenly across the remaining spines and connected by a single link.

Xia topologies trade increased risk and decreased performance for lower flooding amplification, and they have a larger diameter: for M spines the diameter is M plus 2. Some leaves are singly connected, which risks delaying convergence in some failures. A leaf that sees its single link on the flooding topology has failed can compensate by performing a database synchronization check with a different spine, and the same compensation applies if the leaf determines that its connected spine has failed. The benefit of this topology is that the flooding load is easily understood: each node in the spine cycle never receives an update more than twice, and for M leaves and N spines a spine never transmits more than M/N plus 1 updates.

One optimization applies to all of these: if two nodes are adjacent in the flooding topology and there is a set of parallel links between them, any given update MUST be flooded over only one of those links, with the choice of link left to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two shapes are worked out in detail. The minimal one gives every router at least two links in the flooding graph, so no single failure disconnects it. The Xia shape chains the spines through single leaves, so each spine is only lightly loaded, at the cost of a longer route across the graph.

sections.title: Behavioral Specification
sections.content:
The flooding topology MUST include all reachable nodes in the area. If a node's reachability changes, the flooding topology MUST be recalculated, and in centralized mode the Area Leader MUST advertise a new one. If a node becomes disconnected from the current flooding topology but is still reachable, a new flooding topology MUST be calculated. The flooding topology SHOULD be biconnected to provide network resiliency, but this does incur some redundant flooding; Xia topologies are an explicit decision to sacrifice resiliency to avoid redundancy.

Any capable node MAY advertise its eligibility to become the Area Leader. Nodes that are not reachable, or that do not advertise their eligibility, are not eligible. Amongst the eligible nodes, the node with the numerically highest priority is the Area Leader; if several share the highest priority, the node with the numerically highest system identifier in IS-IS, or Router ID in OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, is the Area Leader. This generalizes the Designated Router and Designated Intermediate-System election mechanisms. Not every node needs to be a candidate, since a single candidate suffices for correct operation, but for redundancy it is strongly RECOMMENDED that there be multiple candidates.

In centralized mode the Area Leader MUST advertise algorithm 0 in its Area Leader Sub-TLV, and for dynamic flooding to be enabled it must also compute and advertise a flooding topology. It may update the flooding topology at any time but should not destabilize the network with undue or overly frequent changes; when it advertises a new flooding topology it floods it on both the new and old flooding topologies. In distributed mode the Area Leader MUST advertise a nonzero algorithm, and all nodes in the area that support dynamic flooding and that algorithm MUST compute the flooding topology using it. Nodes that do not support the advertised algorithm continue to use standard flooding and are considered dynamic flooding incapable. Algorithm values in the range 128 to 254 are private, and it is the operator's responsibility to guarantee that all nodes in the area agree on the algorithm.

Nodes that support dynamic flooding MUST use the flooding topology for flooding when possible and MUST NOT revert to standard flooding when a valid flooding topology is available. Received link-state updates, whether received on a link in the flooding topology or not, MUST be flooded on all links in the flooding topology except for the link on which the update was received. A node that finds its current information inconsistent may wait for an implementation-specific time for more information to arrive. If a node determines that adjacencies are to be added to the flooding topology, it should add them and begin flooding on them immediately; if adjacencies are to be removed, it should wait an implementation-specific time before acting, so that new information is flooded promptly and completely.

The document then treats topology events in detail: temporary additions of links, local link additions, node additions, failures of links on and off the flooding topology, node deletions, local link additions and deletions on the flooding topology, treatment of disconnected adjacent nodes, failure of the Area Leader, recovery from multiple failures, and rate-limiting of temporary flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: One router in the area is elected, in much the same way OSPF elects a designated router, and it either works out the flooding graph and publishes it, or tells everyone which algorithm to use so they all work it out the same way. Nodes that fall behind, or that fail, fall back to ordinary flooding, so the network keeps converging.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security issues. Security of routing within a domain is already addressed as part of the routing protocols themselves, and this document proposes no changes to those security architectures.

An attacker could become the Area Leader and introduce a flawed flooding algorithm into the network, compromising the operation of the protocol. The authentication methods described in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 for IS-IS, RFC 2328 and RFC 7474 for OSPFv2, and RFC 5340 and RFC 4552 for OSPFv3 SHOULD be used to prevent such attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The document changes nothing about how routing is authenticated. The one new risk is that an attacker could win the election and hand everyone a bad flooding graph, so the existing protocol authentication should be used.
